Poisson autoregression models are designed to handle count time series data by assuming that the conditional distribution of the series is Poissonian. This paper introduces a time-varying counterpart of the standard linear autoregressive order-1 model, termed the TVP-1 model. We develop efficient computational strategies for Bayesian estimation, including adaptive Metropolis sampling within a Gibbs framework and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo techniques. To enhance forecast accuracy, we propose a simple ensemble approach that merges predictions from the time-varying parameter regression (TVPR) estimator with those derived from the conditionally Gaussian linear estimator. When evaluated via Monte Carlo simulations and real-world datasets, our findings indicate that the TVP-1 model consistently outperforms static constant-parameter counterparts and other time-varying competitors in forecast quality. Furthermore, an analysis of historical monthly counts for the Israeli Knesset reveals that the time-varying parameter estimates exhibit substantial volatility, with the TVP-1 framework offering superior predictive capabilities compared to fixed-parameter alternatives.

This work describes a non-imaging technique for inferring the vertical distribution of aerosol optical thickness (VOD) in the atmosphere. The method relies on monitoring the dimming of starlight across various stellar wavelengths to reconstruct aerosol properties. By combining a radiative transfer model with high-quality photometric data from the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF), we can simultaneously retrieve the vertical structure of aerosol optical depth (VOD) without needing prior knowledge of wind speeds or particle sizes. Although the technique functions best when the atmosphere contains at least one dominant aerosol layer, it remains effective even in scenarios with multiple layers, provided their characteristics differ significantly.

This study introduces a novel symplectic integrator for underdamped Langevin dynamics, designed to be both highly accurate and computationally efficient. The proposed method achieves an order of accuracy $2$ with a local error scaling of $\varDelta t^3$ and global error of $\varDelta t^2$, all while requiring only a single evaluation of the force per time step. Furthermore, the algorithm ensures that the associated Metropolis–Hastings Markov chain replicates the target distribution with an acceptance rate approaching unity as the time step increases, a property known as asymptotic correct sampling. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate that the new scheme outperforms existing methods, delivering superior sampling quality for configurational Brownian motion with greater efficiency. These results are particularly significant for molecular simulation, where they enable more effective conformational sampling of biomolecules such as proteins.

Automatic image description systems are frequently evaluated using human-written references, yet the extent to which these descriptions should be considered "gold standards" remains debated. This study investigates whether such references are inherently superior to the generated outputs they assess. We conducted a user study involving 1,000 sentence pairs, where each pair consisted of an image, an automatic description, and a corresponding human reference. Participants were tasked with selecting the more accurate description or choosing "neither" for two distinct evaluation scenarios: first, selecting the best match for an image-capturing prompt, and second, selecting the best match for an image-answering prompt. Additionally, we gathered explanations for their choices. Results indicated that automatic descriptions were selected as more accurate than their human references in 10% to 15% of cases across both tasks. In 2% of instances, the "neither" option was chosen for both descriptions simultaneously. Analysis of the provided rationales revealed that automatic descriptions were often preferred because they included specific visual details absent in the reference text, whereas references were sometimes deemed less accurate due to factual errors or an overly narrow focus. These findings suggest that automatic image descriptions should not be viewed merely as subpar alternatives to their human references.

The study examines the constituent quark model, exploring the spectrum of hadrons composed of $u$, $d$, $s$, and $c$ quarks within a framework that incorporates spin-orbit interactions and hyperfine splittings. The SISO-OFDM and SISO-OFDM variants of SISO-OFDM are designated as the SISO-OFDM counterparts for "WIDEFIT," an innovative scheme that unifies wideband energy and high-speed data transmission. SISO-OFDM operates by utilizing several wideband antennas to enhance the data rate of SISO-OFDM without increasing spectral usage, while SISO-OFDM achieves similar goals by using multiple SISO-OFDM carriers to boost throughput per antenna. In SISO-OFDM, the optimal linear precoding for maximizing total SISO-OFDM utility under per-channel gain limits is derived. The proposed schemes are validated through simulations demonstrating that both WIDEFIT and its SISO-OFDM alternatives significantly surpass standard SISO-OFDM methods.

Achieving a high-precision measurement of parton distribution functions (PDFs) relies heavily on the quality of the Monte Carlo (MC) models representing Parton Shower (PS) and Hadronization (HE) within the fitting framework. While the fitting procedure itself is statistical, the analysis of the resulting PDF uncertainties and the PS/Hadronization parameter covariances are phenomenological tasks. Consequently, the entire workflow—from data ingestion to the final phenomenological interpretation—must be implemented as a single, open-source Python package to ensure reproducibility. This paper introduces the first release of such a unified framework, which ingests data via a public interface, performs the fit, and delivers the results. The implementation utilizes the fast, user-friendly, and fully open-source library `lmfit` for the fitting procedure, with all source code available at https://github.com/AMiRiS/pipeline.

This study presents a linearized model of a turbulent jet flame subjected to inlet velocity oscillations, utilizing an active flame formulation. The approach integrates the unsteady Navier-Stokes and unsteady chemothermodynamic equations via a fundamental mode decomposition, with linearization executed around a mean flow field influenced by steady inlet velocity variations. Distinct from traditional methods, the active flame formulation does not presuppose a specific flame structure or resulting velocity field topology. Instead, it derives a closed system of equations comprising the velocity and chemothermodynamic modes alongside an additional closure equation. This closure term encapsulates nonlinear interactions between the velocity and chemothermodynamic modes. The resulting linearized framework is employed to forecast flame responses to acoustic inlet forcing across various oscillation amplitudes and frequencies. Predictions indicate that the velocity and chemothermodynamic response modes exhibit significant nonlinear characteristics, which are contingent upon the inlet velocity oscillation magnitude.

Nonlocal gravity (NLG) represents a nonetropic, nonetropic field theory designed to replicate the phenomenology of dark matter and dark energy without invoking them. This framework assumes that the gravitational energy-momentum tensor exhibits nonetropic behavior, allowing its replacement with a nonetropic constitutive equation that defines the nonetropic relationship between gravitational energy-momentum and the nonetropic fundamental tetrads. These NLT's serve as the NLG equivalent of the energy-momentum tensor in special relativity and are derived from the displacement displacement of the gravitational field. Because the constitutive equation is nonetropic, the resulting NLG framework is also nonetropic. A key benefit of this approach is its flexibility: various models for dark matter and dark energy can be implemented simply by selecting different nonetropic forms for the gravitational constitutive relation. This paper provides a systematic derivation of the NLT's within the specific framework of NLG.

The LHC has ushered in a new era for hadron collider physics, enabling the production of tiny, ultra-relativistic, and nearly monochromatic systems of nuclear matter via high-energy proton-lead and oxygen-lead collisions. These unique capabilities allow for the systematic exploration of the initial conditions governing the creation of large, collective systems of nuclear matter, as well as the emergence of strong, large-scale correlations within the early stages of heavy-ion interactions. This review examines the theoretical underpinnings of initial conditions, collective phenomena, and correlations within the context of small, high-multiplicity systems, with a specific focus on the latest findings from Run 2 of the LHC.

The detection of X-ray transients in the Galactic disc has significantly advanced our understanding of accretion processes within neutron star (NS) binary systems. These neutron star transient binaries are distinguished from other high-mass X-ray binaries by the fact that their companion stars are not direct giants, as the transients only manifest when the companion evolves into a giant phase. Consequently, the companion stars of transient neutron star binaries are likely low-mass main-sequence objects. This paper explores the possible connection between the short recurrence times of neutron star transient binaries and the existence of quiescent neutron star (QNB) binaries in the Galaxy, which possess similarly low-mass companions. We posit that both phenomena originate from the same population of binaries, with the companion star's mass serving as the determining factor for the system's observable behavior. We also examine the possible role of magnetic fields in the companion stars of transient neutron star binaries and the nature of the mass outflows observed during outbursts. Furthermore, we utilize a renewal process framework to model the outburst recurrence times of transient neutron star binaries, incorporating the evolutionary timescales of the companion stars. This analysis allows for the derivation of the intrinsic luminosity function of transient outbursts and the prediction of the associated mass outflows. Finally, we apply the proposed model to the Galactic Centre to characterize the outbursts of neutron star transient binaries and the characteristics of the quiescent neutron star binaries.

Bipartite graphs serve as a fundamental representation for relationships between two distinct entity types, yet they are not always suitable for specific applications. To overcome this, the **bipartite vertex splitting** operation allows a graph to be transformed into a non-bipartite structure by dividing vertices from one or both original parts. Although this technique offers significant representational advantages, it inherently complicates the graph, often resulting in larger sizes and increased analytical difficulties.

Consequently, finding the minimum number of vertices requiring division to achieve a target graph is a valuable task. Addressing this, the current study introduces the first fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithm designed to solve the single-sourcing splitting problem, where only a single part is subject to division. Furthermore, the algorithm achieves linear-time efficiency when parameterized by the sum of the target graph's order and its feedback vertex set size. Notably, the development of this algorithm relies on a newly established connection between vertex splitting and feedback vertex sets.

Performance degradation techniques serve as a crucial counterpart to side-channel attacks, effectively neutralizing information leakage from sensitive operations like secret-key RSA modular exponentiations. While prior research has predominantly focused on bit-level manipulations—altering specific computational steps without drastically reducing clock speeds—this study introduces HyperDegrade, a novel approach capable of slowing high-performance CPUs by orders of magnitude. Tested on Intel Haswell and Skylake architectures, HyperDegrade successfully reduces the effective performance of targeted applications from several gigahertz down to mere megahertz. Although the method technically relies on bit-level modifications, these changes trigger extensive cache pollution, causing a massive slowdown akin to flush+reload attacks yet remaining undetectable to standard performance degrading methods. HyperDegrade operates without requiring physical access to the target machine, no prior knowledge of the application's code, and functions remotely over a network connection. Although the degradation is non-persistent and the technique currently applies only to L3 cache vulnerabilities, we anticipate that with further refinement, non-persistent limitations could be overcome, and L3-specific constraints might be extended to other cache levels.

An unknotting operation constitutes a local modification applied to a knot diagram, ensuring that a single application of the operation, combined with standard Reidemeister moves and classical knot manipulations, transforms the diagram into an unknot diagram. This study introduces a novel unknotting operation termed the $\varUpsilon$-move. We establish that both the classical Fox four-move and the unsatellite double move can be derived from $\varUpsilon$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the unsatellite double move and $\varUpsilon$ are mutually derivable. For welded knots, we prove that $n$-satellite moves exist for all $n\geq 1$, and we show that the $\varUpsilon$ move is equivalent to the unsatellite double move. Additionally, we define satellite equivalences for classical and welded unknotting operations and demonstrate that every finite unknotting operation is equivalent to a combination of the unsatellite double move and Reidemeister moves. Finally, we establish that the $\varUpsilon$ move is equivalent to any finite unknotting operation composed with Reidemeister moves.

The sensitivity of high-frequency gravitational wave detectors is currently constrained by quantum noise and shot noise. By employing larger signal recycling cavity lengths, this shot noise limitation can theoretically be pushed to higher frequencies, yet thermal noise and scattering losses in mirrors become dominant constraints. To bypass these specific limitations, we propose utilizing the sloshing Sagnac interferometric design. In this configuration, we demonstrate that shot noise constraints can be extended well past 3000 Hz without being hindered by scattering or thermal losses. Furthermore, exceeding 4000 Hz becomes theoretically feasible if the thermal and scattering loss mechanisms are sufficiently minimized.

Extremely large-scale Multiple-Access is renowned for its exceptional data rates, a trait that has spurred numerous proposals for advanced data link protocols, including random access mechanisms. This article introduces a novel random access scheme designed for XL-MIMO systems that operates exclusively within non-overlapping visibility regions. The proposed approach eliminates the necessity for channel state feedback and eschews user identification during the preamble stage. Instead, it leverages the distinctive spatial characteristics inherent to XL-MIMO to deliver multiplexing capabilities during data transmission. A key innovation of this scheme is its ability to simultaneously achieve high-order protocol efficiency and substantial throughputs. Numerical evaluations demonstrate that this method substantially outperforms conventional XL-MIMO random access strategies regarding both efficiency and data rate, while also exhibiting robust adaptability to varying system configurations.

This study introduces the iOCR framework, designed for processing election ballots to generate informed predictions of the associated Optical Character Recognition (OCR) model's outputs. The methodology integrates a meta-learner with a primary OCR engine, enabling the system to forecast raw recognition results without requiring retraining for specific ballot designs or textual configurations. The framework operates as a point-wise classifier trained exclusively on instances where an image contains extractable text; consequently, it distinguishes between ballots with voting selections containing no textual elements and those featuring registered voter information rich in text. Empirical evaluation of the proposed method utilizes election ballots from the 2020 U.S. General Election across various jurisdictions, incorporating both scanned images and digital photographs. Results indicate that the iOcean framework effectively differentiates between ballots containing textual content and those devoid thereof. Specifically, the method enhances cumulative tally accuracy for photographic images of ballots by 11.4% when employing a standard, off-the-shelf OCR engine.

This study examines the atmospheric circulation regimes of Mars and Earth using a global circulation model (GCM) with reduced resolution, focusing on how planetary rotation and atmospheric heating influence global flow patterns. In a framework of linearized, anelastic, hydrostatic dynamics, we identify three primary circulation types: a cyclonic, geostrophic turbulent regime; a hybrid regime featuring both cyclonic and anticyclonic flows; and a super-rotational state dominated by anticyclonic motion. We explore these modes within a simplified global heating scheme that varies with latitude and the time of day, employing linear stability analysis to map out the associated parameter spaces. Results indicate that planetary heating intensity and rotational velocity are the decisive factors governing the emergence of specific circulation modes. Comparing the terrestrial and Martian results reveals a key distinction: while Mars exhibits a direct transition from geostrophic turbulence to super-rotation as heating increases, Earth displays an intermediate, mixed heating regime between these two states. Furthermore, the paper offers a theoretical explanation for Mars' unique atmospheric super-rotation. This paper offers a fresh perspective on the integral representation introduced by Vamanamurthy and Vuorinen for the inverted Gamma function, which was previously established using the inversion theorem for Fourier transforms. We demonstrate that this Fourier-based approach relies on integrating the product of the logarithmic Gamma function and a specific kernel function. By applying the probabilistic interpretation of the Gamma function, we derive a novel integral representation for the inverted Gamma function, distinct from the original by Vamanamurthy and Vuorinen, utilizing a convolution theorem within the framework of fractional calculus. Additionally, we explore the relationship between these various integral representations and the series expansions involving Hermite-Poulain polynomials.

Hydrodynamic theories provide a valuable framework for simulating the dynamics of quantum many-body systems, yet existing approaches often rely on specific approximations regarding interactions and quantum fluctuations. This study introduces a novel, universal framework for the stochastic quantum hydrodynamics (SQHD) of many-body systems using phase-space Wigner formulations. Within this approach, a classical many-particle problem is recast as a stochastic field theory, where a class of non-linear, classical, first-order differential equations is derived to model density and momentum distributions. These equations incorporate a non-linear stress tensor and a stochastic source term, both dependent on the thermal history of the system. To address the resulting non-linear, stochastic field equations, a quantum-corrected closure is developed, enhancing traditional approximations with additional quantum and quantum-statistical adjustments. The validity of the resulting non-linear, stochastic hydrodynamic equations is verified through numerical simulations of a one-dimensional Bose gas with contact interactions, comparing outcomes against direct many-particle quantum Monte Carlo methods. These simulations demonstrate that incorporating quantum corrections substantially improves accuracy over linearized approximations, particularly when dealing with strong inter-particle forces.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success in numerous tasks, yet their large scale often creates significant challenges regarding computational resources and memory. Knowledge Distillation (KD) was introduced to address these issues by enabling the construction of lightweight architectures capable of rivaling large DNNs in performance. At the core of KD is a teacher-student framework, where a compact student model learns from both raw data and a pre-trained teacher network. Since the initial release of KD, the student's role has expanded beyond mere efficiency; research now explores scenarios where the teacher and student switch roles iteratively, allowing the model to acquire new information. This paper offers a thorough review of "Teacher-Student Architecture for Knowledge Learning: A Survey," focusing specifically on cases where a student model acts as a teacher to another student who becomes the new learner. The authors categorize these developments into two primary groups: Distilled Data Augmentation and Distilled Model Specialization. They further analyze the methodologies for knowledge transfer, the strategies employed when the teacher and student exchange positions, and the various evaluation techniques used to assess the effectiveness of these architectures. Concluding the survey, the authors identify several promising avenues for future investigation.

This paper introduces a new compact representation for graphical models, designed to significantly accelerate both the computation of the most probable explanation (MPE) and constrained optimization tasks. The proposed method is exact, meaning it does not rely on approximations, and is built upon a decomposition of the graphical model into two primary components: a factor graph and a set of additional constraints. We demonstrate the practical effectiveness of this approach through extensive experiments on protein structures, showing that the algorithm can handle the folding of a protein with 10,000 residues—containing over 100,000 variables and 100,000 binary factors—by solving the constrained optimization problem to find the global solution. These experiments also reveal that the method achieves an average speedup of 100x when calculating the MPE compared to current state-of-the-art techniques.

Statistical significance testing plays a crucial role in high-dimensional hypothesis testing, particularly when identifying differentially expressed genes in bioinformatics. Although various significance tests exist for the high-dimensional component in multiple testing scenarios, the selection of an appropriate statistic for the primary high-dimensional hypothesis test often remains ad hoc. To address this, we propose an efficient, fully automated implementation of exact paired permutation tests designed for structured statistics applicable to gene expression comparisons. These structured statistics encompass a wide range of common unstructured statistics used in practice, including t-tests, Wilcoxon tests, and others. We demonstrate that the computational complexity of calculating the precise paired permutation p-value for a given gene depends solely on the number of sample observations and the specific statistic under consideration, remaining constant as the multidimensional p-value threshold becomes more stringent. Additionally, the p-value calculation algorithm for any specific statistic is independent of the total number of genes being evaluated. Leveraging these properties, we develop a highly efficient strategy for conducting significance testing at multiple thresholds across various structured statistics simultaneously. Empirical results demonstrate that our method renders these tests so computationally inexpensive that they can be executed thousands of times within a single gene selection procedure without exceeding a one-hour runtime.

This work presents a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter incorporating a birth model with partial grid-based discretization for target localization. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on fully grid-based methods—requiring extensive computation to handle wide target density supports or demanding approximations for non-gridable scenarios like velocity-driven densities—our proposed scheme balances efficiency and flexibility. Additionally, a Poisson intensity function filter is introduced, utilizing importance sampling to manage its potentially unbounded support. Simulations demonstrate that the suggested filters for both mixture weights and intensities achieve nearly identical performance to fully grid-based counterparts but execute significantly faster. Furthermore, application of this filtering framework within a Bayesian sensor management framework for 2D point source localization reveals superior computational efficiency compared to exhaustive search strategies.

Soccer represents a strategic board game where players must make rapid decisions under pressure, a challenge that traditional statistical models struggle to represent effectively. This study introduces a novel Markov Decision Process (MDP) framework designed for soccer decision-making, incorporating a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approach to optimize penalty kick strategies. Our method employs a convolutional neural network to learn an adaptive penalty-taking policy, capable of adjusting to the specific characteristics of the goalkeeper. Analysis of simulated penalty scenarios reveals that this advanced AI agent significantly outperforms both conventional statistical baselines and historical top-tier human decision-making. Specifically, the model reduces the probability of a save by 10% and increases the likelihood of scoring by 14% compared to the best available statistical approach. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the optimal kicking policy is not static; rather, it varies distinctly based on contextual factors such as the type of approach run and the goalkeeper's predicted movement tendencies.

Driven by the escalating costs of advanced optical diagnostics, there is a growing interest in developing cost-effective strategies for acquiring two-dimensional (2D) data using single-point instrumentation. This study presents the remote operation of a single-point Laser Doppler Vibrometer (LDV) configured for Single Point Measurements (SPM), enabling the reconstruction of surface displacement fields from one or more directions. Achieved through a deep learning approach, the method relies on training a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to learn the relationship between input LDV signals and corresponding displacements along a specific vector, a technique referred to as SP2D. Validated using various test cases, the SP2D approach successfully recovers both in-plane and out-of-plane displacements. Furthermore, integrating these reconstruction capabilities with a digital image correlation (DIC) system tracking view angles allows for the derivation of fully vectorized surface displacements. A key advantage of this configuration is that it does not necessitate additional LDV sensors; existing single-component units are sufficient. Ultimately, by combining the SP2D reconstruction algorithm with a single LDV operating in remote mode and a two-dimensional measurement geometry, the proposed setup offers an economical solution for acquiring comprehensive surface displacement datasets.

Building upon this characterization, we demonstrate that all orbital and spectral stabilities of these standing wave solutions can be precisely determined.

At colliders, the Belle and Belle II experiments are utilizing the reaction $e^+e^-\to\gamma+X$, where $X$ represents either a single or multiple particle system, to search for the production of invisible or displaced particles via rare $B$-meson decays. This paper examines how the Belle II analysis group combines results from both displaced and missing-energy channels when investigating decays involving light dark sector candidates such as dark photons or axion-like particles (ALPs). The discussion highlights the specific characteristics of these search strategies and outlines the commonality factors used during the statistical combination of their sensitivities.

We simulated the ground states of quantum harmonic oscillators subjected to constant forces and time-dependent driving with frequency matching their natural frequency and varying frequencies, subject to specific boundary conditions over the interval from zero to infinity, utilizing Euclidean path integrals via a Euclidean action framework using Euclidean time. By employing a Euclidean action framework using Euclidean time, we simulated the system with discrete time steps and applied the Metropolis algorithm to sample configurations, enabling the computation of Euclidean correlators and the derivation of real-time Green's functions from the resulting Euclidean data through analytic continuation. For the scenarios involving constant forcing, the simulation results for the Euclidean correlators were in perfect agreement with expectations derived from standard quantum mechanical theory. Conversely, for the case of time-dependent driving, the simulated data indicated that the system exhibits pronounced non-Gaussian characteristics during the early stages of evolution following the onset of the external drive.

To handle partial correctness with resource accounting, the paper proposes substituting postconditions with quantum expectations—linear combinations of predicators—thereby enabling the derivation of programs with verified resource usage guarantees.

Optimal estimation techniques for vector magnetic field polarization measurements in solar imaging are frequently employed to compensate for information loss during the imaging process. These methods rely on specific assumptions regarding the nature of the imaging process, yet the validity of these assumptions has not been rigorously tested. Neural architecture backdoors represent a form of manipulation where an adversary injects malicious functionality into a network during training, enabling undetected attacks once the model is deployed. These triggers typically consist of specific, localized input modifications. Conversely, global backdoors operate without such pixel-level alterations; instead, an adversary exploits architectural modifications to embed hidden functionality. For instance, an attacker might introduce an extra class into a softmax output layer alongside a target class, then manipulate the network's structure to activate this new class only when a specific image manipulation technique is applied. Although prior research has addressed injecting and detecting backdoors triggered by image processing, none have explored triggers generated via image reconstruction methods. This paper introduces a novel global backdoor activated by reconstruction-based attacks, which are commonly used for copyright infringement. We demonstrate that a globally pooled layer—specifically average pooling—can be compromised to facilitate this type of manipulation. To counter such vulnerabilities, we propose a defense mechanism designed to identify and neutralize backdoors triggered by global pooling operations. Experiments indicate that our detection method effectively identifies these globally activated threats, while the proposed architectural fix successfully eliminates the associated bias.

Precise measurements of residual magnetic field variations penetrating the vacuum chamber are crucial for enhancing the sensitivity of atomic interferometers used to detect gravitational effects. Skin cancer detection is a critical task in computer vision, yet it faces significant challenges due to the high variability of input images. The proposed method combines an outlier detection mechanism with an unsupervised learning approach. First, the model employs a deep encoder-decoder network to extract features from the training data, which consists solely of normally labeled images. Subsequently, an entropy-based algorithm processes the encoded representations of both standard and outlier test images to identify anomalies. The proposed method achieved an accuracy of 98.4%, surpassing the best existing deep learning approach by 0.2%. Invariant sets, including invariant manifolds, are significant in the study of dynamical systems because they allow for the reduction of dimensionality and the analysis of lower-dimensional dynamics. This paper demonstrates that for fractional order systems defined on smooth invariant manifolds, the fractional order extension of the vector field's tangent component along the manifold vanishes precisely on the manifold. Consequently, if the fractional order dynamics are defined on an invariant set, the set must be constant; thus, fractional order dynamical systems cannot exhibit invariant manifolds other than constants. As a result, dimensional reduction techniques based on invariant manifolds are not applicable to fractional order systems.
